content: 1. Gatifloxacin is the fluoroquinolone most likely to cause dysglycemia, while moxifloxacin is the least likely. Levofloxacin enhances the effects of regular human insulin through pharmacodynamic synergy. Use caution and monitor closely, as quinolone antibiotics can lead to hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia. 2. Both ketoconazole and levofloxacin prolong the QTc interval. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 3. Levofloxacin, when combined with ketoprofen, ketorolac (including intranasal forms), or other NSAIDs, increases the risk of central nervous system (CNS) stimulation and seizures. This occurs due to the displacement of GABA from its receptors in the brain. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is advised. 4. Lanthanum carbonate reduces levofloxacin levels by binding cations in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Administer oral quinolones at least 1 hour before or 4 hours after lanthanum to avoid this interaction. This interaction applies only to oral forms of quinolones. 5. Lapatinib, lenvatinib, leuprolide, and levoketoconazole, when co-administered with levofloxacin, increase the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. Lenvatinib prescribing information specifically recommends close ECG monitoring when used with QT-prolonging drugs. Leuprolide also increases the risk of torsades de pointes. 6. Levofloxacin decreases the effectiveness of oral contraceptives containing levonorgestrel, ethinyl estradiol, or ferrous bisglycinate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of hormones. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are advised. 7. Lithium, lofepramine, lumefantrine, and other drugs that prolong the QTc interval, when combined with levofloxacin, increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 8. Magnesium salts (chloride, citrate, hydroxide, oxide, sulfate, or supplements) reduce levofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption or forming insoluble complexes. Administer magnesium 2 hours before or 2 hours after levofloxacin to avoid this interaction. This applies only to oral forms of both agents. 9. Mavorixafor and levofloxacin both prolong the QTc interval. Mavorixafor causes concentration-dependent QTc prolongation, and QTc monitoring is recommended in patients with risk factors. Dose reduction or discontinuation of mavorixafor may be required. 10. Levofloxacin increases the effects of metformin, miglitol, nateglinide, pioglitazone, repaglinide, rosiglitazone, saxagliptin, and sitagliptin through pharmacodynamic synergy. Use caution and monitor closely, as quinolone antibiotics may cause hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia. Gatifloxacin is most likely to cause dysglycemia, while moxifloxacin is least likely. 11. Methadone, mifepristone, mirtazapine, and other QTc-prolonging drugs, when combined with levofloxacin, increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Alternatives should be considered when available. 12. Co-administration of quinolone antibiotics (e.g., levofloxacin) with corticosteroids (e.g., methylprednisolone, mometasone, prednisolone, prednisone, or triamcinolone) increases the risk of tendon rupture. Use caution and monitor closely. 13. Levofloxacin decreases the levels or effects of mestranol and sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering intestinal flora or metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. For sodium picosulfate combinations, administer levofloxacin at least 2 hours before and no less than 6 hours after to avoid magnesium chelation. 14. Drugs such as nilotinib, nortriptyline, octreotide, olanzapine, osilodrostat, osimertinib, oxaliplatin, and others that prolong the QTc interval, when combined with levofloxacin, increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Periodic ECG and electrolyte monitoring are advised for patients on QTc-prolonging drugs. 15. Levofloxacin, when combined with NSAIDs such as oxaprozin, piroxicam, sulindac, or tolmetin, increases the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures due to GABA receptor displacement. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 16. Posaconazole, primiquine, prochlorperazine, promethazine, quetiapine, quinine, quizartinib, ranolazine, rilpivirine, risperidone, romidepsin, sorafenib, sunitinib, tacrolimus, telavancin, thioridazine, trazodone, triclobendazole, and other QTc-prolonging drugs, when combined with levofloxacin, increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. 17. Sucralfate decreases levofloxacin levels by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Sulfamethoxazole and levofloxacin both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Selpercatinib and levofloxacin increase the risk of QTc prolongation. Use caution and monitor closely. 20. Sertraline and levofloxacin both prolong the QTc interval. Use caution and monitor closely. 21. Levofloxacin decreases the effects of phenytoin by an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely, as there are case reports of quinolones increasing phenytoin levels. 22. Levofloxacin and sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate combinations decrease each other's levels by inhibiting GI absorption. Administer levofloxacin at least 2 hours before and no less than 6 hours after to avoid chelation with magnesium. 23. Levofloxacin and sulindac increase the risk of CNS stimulation and seizures due to GABA receptor displacement. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended.
